analysis.one_liner: Requires chain restaurants and vending machines to post calorie, fat, and sodium information.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee for the rest of the 108th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal food law to require chain restaurants with 20 or more outlets to print calories, saturated plus trans fat, and sodium next to every item on menus and menu boards, and to require calorie counts on vending machines. The Health and Human Services Secretary would have had to write implementing rules within a year. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers eating out or buying from vending machines, who would see nutrition information at the point of purchase instead of having to ask or look it up. The bill's findings note that about a third of calories and nearly half of food dollars are spent on restaurant food, where nutrition labeling is generally not required. People managing weight, heart disease risk, or blood pressure would be the direct beneficiaries, and families and governments who bear obesity-related health costs would share the benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Requires chains with 20 or more outlets under the same name to list calories, saturated plus trans fat, and sodium next to each menu item, in a clear and conspicuous manner.
Requires vending machines and restaurant menu boards to display the calorie count of each item.

Directs the Health and Human Services Secretary to propose implementing regulations within 12 months and issue final rules within 24 months, with the proposed rules automatically becoming final if the deadline is missed.
Lets states and local governments require additional nutrition information beyond the federal floor, and leaves restaurants free to post more than the minimum.

analysis.who_pays: Large chain restaurants and vending machine operators, who would bear the cost of calculating and printing nutrition information for menu items. Chains with fewer than 20 locations and independent restaurants would be exempt.

drawbacks.text: Chain restaurants would face real compliance costs to analyze every menu item for calories, saturated plus trans fat, and sodium, and reprint menus when recipes change; small chains just under the 20-store threshold would face pressure near the cutoff.
Menu labels alone may not change what people order; the bill's own findings note that labeling helps, but the strongest evidence at the time came from packaged-food labels rather than restaurants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is information at the moment of choice for food that makes up a large share of American diets, at a modest and one-time cost to large chains. The main honest objection is that posting numbers does not guarantee anyone reads them, but the bill's own findings cite evidence that label users change purchasing decisions. The cost falls on a concentrated industry; the benefit is broadly distributed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro and seven other House Democrats introduced the Menu Education and Labeling Act on November 5, 2003.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On November 14, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was taken.
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on March 10, 2004, and the bill had 24 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never advanced to a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large chain restaurants and vending operators avoided point-of-sale labeling requirements and the costs of compliance for the rest of that Congress. Consumers who wanted nutrition information at the counter gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.role: Sponsor, House Ranking Member on the Appropriations Agriculture Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor in March 2004.

for.name: Reps. Waxman, Brown of Ohio, Eshoo, Emanuel, Thompson, Jones of Ohio, and Owens
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in November 2003 and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.

against.name: Restaurant and vending industry
against.what_they_did: Would have borne compliance costs under the bill; the industry opposed menu-labeling mandates in this era, though no lobbying appears in the provided record.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached the floor, so no votes were ever cast on it.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to print calories, saturated plus trans fat, and sodium next to every menu item, a compliance cost with no offsetting revenue. Their business benefits when nutrition information stays off menus, so their interest ran against the consumers the bill served.
The bill would have required calorie labels on items sold in vending machines. Small compliance burden, but it removes an information gap that favors impulse purchases of less healthy items.

Establishments with fewer than 20 outlets were exempt, avoiding compliance costs. They could also voluntarily provide nutrition information or face stricter state and local rules if states chose to impose them.
